t: Natural Regions of the World and How They Connect
d: How climate, rock, soil, water and life combine into distinct natural regions, from the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the Sahara, and how to explore their links across this encyclopedia.
x: Geographers divide the land into natural regions : areas where similar climate, landforms, soils, vegetation and wildlife occur together and shape similar ways of farming and living. The Regions catalog holds 99 of them, each linked to its countries , climate zones , soils , landforms , species and crops . The chain of causes # Climate → water → soil → life → people 1. **Latitude and air circulation** set the basic climate: rainy tropics, dry subtropical deserts, stormy mid-latitudes, cold poles. See [Climate zones explained](/wiki/climate/climate-zones-explained.html). 2. **Mountains and oceans** modify it: the Western Ghats soak the Konkan and leave the Deccan dry; the cold Humboldt Current creates the Atacama. 3. **Rainfall and temperature** decide **weathering and leaching**, and with the **parent rock** they make the soil: black regur on Deccan basalt, red soils on granite, deep chernozem under steppe grass, leached laterite under monsoon rain, and frozen gelisols in the Arctic. See [What is soil?](/wiki/soil/what-is-soil.html). 4. **Climate and soil** decide the **vegetation**: rainforest, savanna, steppe, taiga, tundra, desert scrub. 5. **Vegetation** decides the **wildlife**: tigers in monsoon forests, saiga on the steppe, orangutans in Bornean rainforest. 6. Together they decide **what people can farm**: rice on wet alluvial deltas, wheat on cool dry plains, millets and pulses in semi-arid lands, tea and coffee on wet hill slopes, dates in oases. t: How Land Forms: Plates, Mountains and Erosion
d: Continents drift, collide and tear apart; rain, ice and wind wear them down. The two forces together build every landscape on Earth.
x: Earth’s land covers about 148.9 million km² , roughly 29% of the planet’s surface. Every hill, plain and plateau on it is the result of a tug-of-war between two engines: internal forces (plate tectonics and volcanism) that push land up, and external forces (weathering, rivers, glaciers, wind and waves) that wear it down. Land in numbers Land area: ~148.9 million km² (29% of Earth’s surface) Highest point: Mount Everest, 8,849 m Lowest dry land: the Dead Sea shore, about −430 m and falling Average land elevation: ~840 m Oldest rocks: ~4.0 billion years (Acasta Gneiss, Canada); oldest mineral grains ~4.4 billion years (Jack Hills zircons, Australia) Plate tectonics: the engine underneath # The outer shell of Earth, the lithosphere , is broken into about 15 major plates that float on the hotter, softer asthenosphere . They move 2–10 cm a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. What happens at their edges shapes the land: The three kinds of plate boundary - **Convergent (colliding).** When two continents collide, neither sinks, so crust crumples upward. The Indian plate hit Asia around 50 million years ago and is still pushing north about 4–5 cm a year, raising the **Himalaya** and the **Tibetan Plateau**. When ocean crust meets a continent it dives under (subducts), producing volcanic ranges such as the **Andes**. - **Divergent (pulling apart).** Where plates separate, the crust thins, faults and sinks into rift valleys. The **East African Rift** is slowly splitting Africa; in tens of millions of years it may become a new ocean, as the Red Sea already is. - **Transform (sliding past).** Plates grind sideways, building earthquakes rather than mountains, as along California's **San Andreas Fault**. The supercontinent Pangaea assembled about 335 million years ago and began breaking apart about 200 million years ago. India broke away from Gondwana, crossed the ocean faster than any other continent, and collided with Asia; that is why fossils of the same plants ( Glossopteris ) and reptiles are found in India, Africa, Antarctica and Australia. Volcanoes and flood basalts # Volcanoes build land directly. Some of the largest land features are flood basalts : vast stacks of lava erupted over short geological periods. India’s Deccan Traps covered around 500,000 km² of west-central India about 66 million years ago, close to the time of the dinosaur extinction. Their weathering created India’s fertile black cotton soil . Iceland, Hawaii and the Andaman Sea’s Barren Island are still growing today. The forces that wear land down # Weathering breaks rock where it stands: by freezing and thawing (frost wedging), by heating and cooling, by roots, and by chemical reactions with water and carbon dioxide (which dissolves limestone into karst caves and towers). Rivers carry the debris. The Ganges and Brahmaputra together deliver around a billion tonnes of sediment a year, building the world’s largest delta in Bangladesh and West Bengal. Glaciers scrape U-shaped valleys, fjords and lakes; the Ice Ages left the lake-studded plains of Canada and Finland. Wind shapes dunes and carries dust; wind-blown silt ( loess ) forms some of the most fertile farmland in China, Ukraine and the US Midwest. Waves cut cliffs, beaches and sea stacks. Landforms by origin # Origin Examples Fold mountains (collision) Himalaya, Alps, Zagros Volcanic mountains Kilimanjaro, Fuji, Andes Block mountains and rift valleys Vosges, Black Forest, East African Rift Plateaus (uplift or lava) Tibetan, Deccan, Colorado, Ethiopian River plains and deltas Indo-Gangetic Plain, Nile delta, Mekong delta Glacial landforms Fjords of Norway, Great Lakes, moraines Aeolian (wind) landforms Sahara ergs, Thar dunes, loess plateaus Karst Meghalaya caves, Ha Long Bay, Guilin Why this matters for people # Landforms decide where rain falls (mountains force air to rise and drop its moisture, leaving a dry rain shadow behind), which soils form, which crops grow and where people live. Most of humanity lives on low river plains and coasts, because flat land with deep alluvial soil and water is the easiest to farm. Next: Mountains and plateaus · Browse every landform . Sources: USGS: This Dynamic Earth · Wikipedia: Plate tectonics · Wikipedia: Deccan Traps

d: How mountains rise, why their tops are cold and snowy, how altitude creates climate zones stacked like floors of a building, and why plateaus feed and water billions.
x: Mountains cover about a quarter of Earth’s land and are home to roughly 1.1 billion people, yet they supply between half and most of the world’s fresh water , earning them the name “water towers”. Plateaus, high flat tablelands, include some of the most farmed and mined land on Earth. How mountains rise # Four ways to build a mountain - **Fold mountains** form where plates collide and crust buckles: the Himalaya, Alps, Atlas and the ancient Appalachians and Aravallis. - **Volcanic mountains** are piles of erupted lava and ash: Kilimanjaro, Fuji, Mauna Kea, Elbrus. - **Fault-block mountains** are slabs of crust pushed up along faults, like the Sierra Nevada in California. - **Dome and residual mountains** are bulges of rock or the hard remains of older ranges worn down by erosion, such as the Nilgiris' older rocks or the Ozarks. Young ranges are tall and jagged (the Himalaya is still rising ~4 mm a year at Everest). Old ranges like the Aravalli (over 1.5 billion years) are worn down to rounded hills. Mountain tops: life at the edge # Air cools by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb (the environmental lapse rate), and holds less oxygen: at Everest’s summit air pressure is about a third of sea level. As a result mountain slopes are stacked into altitudinal zones that mirror the trip from equator to pole: Zone (Himalaya, approx.) Elevation Vegetation and land use Tropical/subtropical < 1,000 m Sal forest, rice, tea in the foothills Temperate 1,000–3,000 m Oak, rhododendron, apples, potatoes, terraced fields Subalpine 3,000–4,000 m Fir, birch, juniper; summer pastures (bugyals) Alpine 4,000–5,000 m Meadows, cushion plants, yak grazing Nival (snow) > 5,000 m Permanent snow, glaciers, bare rock The snow line , above which snow lasts all year, sits at ~5,000–6,000 m in the Himalaya, ~3,000 m in the Alps and at sea level near the poles. Rising temperatures are pushing snow lines and tree lines upward, shrinking the alpine zone and its specialised species. Mountains make weather # When moist wind meets a range it rises, cools and drops rain or snow on the windward side ( orographic rainfall ). The other side lies in a dry rain shadow . Examples: - The Western Ghats catch the southwest monsoon, giving the Konkan and Malabar coasts 2,500–5,000 mm a year, while Pune, just inland, gets ~700 mm. - The Himalaya block cold Central Asian air from India and wring the monsoon dry, leaving Ladakh and Tibet as cold deserts. - The Andes create the Atacama on one side (with the cold Humboldt Current) and drench the Amazon slope on the other. Plateaus # Great plateaus Tibetan Plateau: ~2.5 million km², average ~4,500 m; source of the Indus, Ganges’ tributaries, Brahmaputra, Yangtze, Yellow, Mekong and Salween rivers. Holds the largest ice outside the poles, sometimes called the “Third Pole”. Deccan Plateau: most of peninsular India, tilted east so its rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) flow to the Bay of Bengal. Black soil in the northwest, red soil in the south and east. Chota Nagpur Plateau: India’s richest mineral belt (coal, iron ore, mica, bauxite). Altiplano: ~3,750 m in Bolivia and Peru, home of Lake Titicaca and potato and quinoa domestication. Ethiopian Highlands: “roof of Africa”, source of the Blue Nile; teff and coffee originated here. Colorado Plateau: carved into the Grand Canyon. Pressures on mountains # Glacier loss: glaciers lost 408 ± 132 gigatonnes of ice in 2025 alone, and loss has accelerated from under 100 Gt a year in 1976–1995 to about 390 Gt a year in 2016–2025 (WGMS). That threatens the meltwater many Asian rivers rely on in the dry season. Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) , such as the 2013 Kedarnath and 2023 Sikkim floods. Landslides made worse by road cutting and deforestation, e.g. Joshimath’s subsidence (2023) and the Wayanad debris flows (2024). Browse mountains, ranges and plateaus · Next: Deserts of the world . Sources: FAO: Mountain Partnership · WGMS: Global glacier state · Wikipedia: Tibetan Plateau

t: Deserts of the World: Hot, Cold, Coastal and Polar
d: A desert is defined by dryness, not heat. Why deserts form, the five main kinds, how life and people survive in them, and how deserts are growing and shrinking.
x: A desert is land that receives less than about 250 mm of precipitation a year , or where evaporation far exceeds rainfall. By that definition about a third of Earth’s land is desert or semi-desert, and the largest desert of all is not the Sahara but Antarctica . Why deserts form # Five causes of dryness 1. **Subtropical high pressure.** Air rising at the equator descends around 20–30° north and south, warming and drying as it sinks. This belt holds the Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Kalahari and Australian deserts. 2. **Rain shadows.** Mountains strip moisture from wind: the Gobi and Taklamakan lie behind the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau; Patagonia lies behind the Andes. 3. **Distance from the sea (continentality).** Air crossing thousands of kilometres of land loses moisture; Central Asia's Kyzylkum and Karakum are far from any ocean. 4. **Cold ocean currents.** Cold water cools the air above it so it cannot rise and rain. The Humboldt Current feeds the Atacama; the Benguela Current feeds the Namib. These coastal deserts are often foggy but almost rainless. 5. **Polar cold.** Freezing air holds little moisture, so Antarctica and the high Arctic are deserts. Kinds of desert # Kind Examples Features Hot subtropical Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Great Victoria, Mojave Summer days above 45 °C; cold nights; sand seas (ergs) and rocky plains (regs, hamadas) Cold (mid-latitude) Gobi, Taklamakan, Ladakh, Patagonian Freezing winters, hot summers Coastal fog Atacama, Namib Cool, foggy, almost no rain Polar Antarctica, Arctic Ice-covered or bare frozen ground Salt deserts and flats Rann of Kutch, Salar de Uyuni, Dasht-e Kavir Evaporated lakes and seasonal floods Desert records Largest hot desert: Sahara , ~9.2 million km², about the size of the USA Driest non-polar place: Atacama , where some stations average under 1 mm a year Oldest desert: Namib , dry for ~55–80 million years Highest air temperature recorded: 56.7 °C, Death Valley , 1913 (disputed by some climatologists) Highest land-surface temperatures: ~70 °C+ measured by satellite in Iran’s Lut Desert Most populous desert: the Thar , with roughly 80+ people per km² in places The Thar and India’s dry west # The Thar Desert covers about 200,000 km² across western Rajasthan, parts of Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab, and Pakistan’s Sindh. Rainfall falls from about 500 mm in the east to under 100 mm near Jaisalmer, almost all in July–September. Communities adapted with stepwells ( baoris ), village ponds ( johads ), underground tanks ( kundis/tankas ) and drought-hardy crops: pearl millet (bajra) , cluster bean ( guar ), moth bean and the desert tree khejri ( Prosopis cineraria ). The Indira Gandhi Canal now irrigates parts of the desert, turning sand into wheat and mustard fields but also causing waterlogging and salinity. Life in deserts # Desert plants store water (cacti, euphorbias), grow deep roots (acacias, khejri), or live as seeds waiting years for rain. Animals avoid daytime heat, get water from food and concentrate their urine; the dromedary camel can lose up to a quarter of its body water and recover. Fog-basking beetles in the Namib drink droplets that condense on their backs. Deserts change # The Sahara was green about 11,000–5,000 years ago during the African Humid Period, with lakes, hippos and cattle herders, because a slight wobble in Earth’s orbit strengthened the monsoon. Rock art of swimmers survives in Egypt’s Gilf Kebir. Today, desertification (land degradation in drylands, mainly from overgrazing, poor farming and drought) threatens drylands home to about two billion people. Up to 40% of the world’s land is degraded, according to the UN. See land degradation . Restoration works: Niger’s farmers regrew trees on ~5 million hectares by protecting stumps, and China’s Loess Plateau project restored eroded hills. Browse all deserts and other landforms . Sources: USGS: Deserts · Wikipedia: Thar Desert · Wikipedia: African humid period

d: About a tenth of Earth's land lies under ice and a further quarter of the northern land is frozen underground. How the cryosphere works, why it is shrinking and what that means for water and sea level.
x: The cryosphere is every part of Earth where water is frozen: snow, glaciers, ice caps, ice sheets, sea ice, lake and river ice, and frozen ground (permafrost). On land, glaciers and ice sheets cover about 10% of the surface and store about 69% of the world’s fresh water . Snow # Snow forms when water vapour freezes directly onto ice nuclei in clouds below 0 °C. Seasonal snow covers up to about a third of Earth’s land in the northern winter. Its brilliant white surface reflects 80–90% of sunlight (high albedo ), so less snow means more heat absorbed, a feedback that speeds warming. In the Himalaya, Hindu Kush and Alps, spring snowmelt fills rivers just as farmers plant crops. Glaciers: rivers of ice # A glacier forms where more snow falls each winter than melts each summer. Over decades the snow compresses into dense blue ice that flows downhill under its own weight, carving U-shaped valleys and leaving moraines. The world's ice Antarctic Ice Sheet: ~14 million km², up to 4.8 km thick; enough ice to raise sea level ~58 m Greenland Ice Sheet: ~1.7 million km²; enough to raise sea level ~7 m Mountain glaciers: ~200,000 of them; the Himalaya–Karakoram–Hindu Kush hold the most ice outside the poles, the “Third Pole” India’s longest glaciers include Siachen (~76 km) and Gangotri (~30 km), source of the Bhagirathi/Ganga Glaciers are retreating fast # Glaciers lost 408 ± 132 gigatonnes of ice in hydrological year 2025, equal to about 1.1 mm of global sea-level rise, according to the World Glacier Monitoring Service; loss has risen from under 100 Gt a year in 1976–1995 to about 390 Gt a year in 2016–2025. Since 1975 the cumulative loss is about 9,583 Gt , or 26.4 mm of sea-level rise. 2025 was the fourth year in a row in which every one of the world’s 19 glacier regions lost mass (Copernicus). Global glacier mass loss (Gt per year) 100 Gt 1976–1995 390 Gt 2016–2025 avg 408 Gt 2025 Source: WGMS / World Glacier Monitoring Service (1976–95 shown as upper bound of Why it matters: About 1.9 billion people depend on water from the Hindu Kush Himalaya. In the short run melting raises river flows (“peak water”); in the long run, as glaciers shrink, summer and dry-season flows fall. Glacial lakes swell and can burst (GLOFs): Kedarnath 2013 and South Lhonak in Sikkim 2023 were catastrophic examples. Permafrost # Permafrost is ground that stays at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years. It underlies about 15% of the exposed land of the Northern Hemisphere (Siberia, Alaska, northern Canada, the Tibetan Plateau). Arctic permafrost stores roughly 1,400–1,600 billion tonnes of carbon, about twice what is in the atmosphere. As it thaws: - roads, pipelines and buildings tilt and crack; - the ground slumps into thermokarst lakes and craters; - microbes decompose old organic matter and release CO₂ and methane, a feedback that adds to warming. Tundra and snowy regions # Above the tree line lies tundra : treeless plains of mosses, lichens, sedges and dwarf shrubs, with a growing season of 50–60 days. It is grazed by reindeer, caribou and musk oxen and herded by peoples such as the Sámi and Nenets. In the Himalaya, the cold deserts of Ladakh and Spiti grow barley, peas and apricots in short summers using glacier-fed channels, and engineer Sonam Wangchuk’s “ice stupas” store winter meltwater as artificial glaciers for spring irrigation. Browse ice sheets, glaciers and tundra . Sources: WGMS: Global glacier state · Copernicus: Global Climate Highlights · NSIDC: All about frozen ground

t: Forests, Grasslands and Wetlands: The Living Land
d: The biomes that cover the green part of the land, from rainforest and taiga to savanna, steppe, mangroves and peat, how they work, and how much of each is left.
x: A biome is a large region defined by its climate and the vegetation it supports. Land biomes range from dense rainforest to open grassland and wetland, and each supports its own soils, animals and kinds of farming. Forests # Forests cover about 4.06 billion hectares , roughly 31% of land (FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020). The main forest biomes - **Tropical rainforest** (Amazon, Congo, Borneo, Western Ghats, Northeast India): over 2,000 mm of rain a year, no cold season, the richest biodiversity on land. Nutrients are locked in the trees, not the soil, so cleared rainforest land often loses fertility within a few years. - **Tropical dry and monsoon forest** (central India, Southeast Asia): trees such as **teak** and **sal** shed leaves in the dry season. - **Temperate deciduous forest** (Europe, eastern USA, eastern China): oak, beech and maple on fertile brown soils; much of it was cleared for farming centuries ago. - **Temperate rainforest** (Pacific Northwest, southern Chile, New Zealand). - **Boreal forest (taiga):** the largest land biome, across Russia, Scandinavia and Canada; conifers on acidic podzols; a huge carbon store now hit by wildfires (Canada lost about 18 million hectares to fire in 2023). - **Mediterranean woodland and scrub** (maquis, chaparral, fynbos): fire-adapted shrubs, olives and cork oak. Deforestation, then and now # The world lost about 420 million hectares of forest between 1990 and 2020, mostly converted to farmland and pasture. Hope comes from the Amazon: Brazil’s official PRODES system measured 3,335 km² cleared in August 2025–July 2026, a 41.8% drop and the lowest since monitoring began in 1988, while clearing in the Cerrado fell about 24%. Amazon deforestation in Brazil (PRODES, km²/yr) 0 2,500 5,000 7,500 10,000 12,500 15,000 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 2019: 10,129 2020: 10,851 2021: 13,038 2022: 11,594 2023: 9,001 2024: 6,288 2025: 5,796 2026: 3,335 Source: INPE PRODES (Aug–Jul years; 2026 preliminary) Grasslands # Grasslands cover about a quarter to two-fifths of land depending on definition and include: - Tropical savanna : grasses with scattered trees (Serengeti, Sahel margins, Deccan scrub, northern Australia), shaped by fire and grazing. - Temperate grassland : the Eurasian steppe , North American prairie , Argentine pampas and South African veld . Their deep, dark mollisol and chernozem soils make them the world’s breadbaskets, which is why most have been ploughed. - Montane grassland : alpine meadows and Indian shola -grassland mosaics in the Nilgiris. India’s grasslands, such as the Banni in Kutch and the Terai grasslands, are often wrongly classed as “wasteland” and planted with trees; they are home to the great Indian bustard, blackbuck and wild ass. Wetlands # Wetlands cover only about 6% of land but store a third of soil carbon and filter water, buffer floods and nurture fisheries. About 35% of wetlands have been lost since 1970. Great wetlands Pantanal (Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay): the largest tropical wetland Sundarbans (India, Bangladesh): the largest mangrove forest, home of the Bengal tiger Okavango Delta (Botswana): a river that floods the Kalahari The Sudd (South Sudan): a vast Nile swamp Peatlands of Indonesia, the Congo Basin and Siberia: waterlogged soils packed with carbon India’s Ramsar sites include Chilika Lake, Keoladeo, Loktak and the Sundarbans Browse forests, grasslands and wetlands · Climate zones . Sources: FAO: Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 · Ramsar Convention: Global Wetland Outlook · Wikipedia: Biome

d: From the Himalaya to the Thar, the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Deccan, the coasts and the islands, a tour of India's land, soils, rainfall and the crops each region grows.
x: India covers 3.287 million km² , about 2.4% of the world’s land, yet supports roughly 17–18% of its people. That is possible because of fertile river plains, a monsoon that delivers most of the year’s water in four months, and soils that range from deep alluvium to basalt-derived black earth. India at a glance Highest point: Kangchenjunga , 8,586 m (Sikkim) Lowest point: Kuttanad , Kerala, about −2.2 m (farmed below sea level) Wettest places: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji , Meghalaya, ~11,800 mm a year Driest: western Rajasthan and Ladakh, under 100 mm in places Net sown area: about 140 million hectares, roughly 43% of the land, among the highest shares of any large country 1. The Himalaya and the northern mountains # A 2,400 km arc of fold mountains in three parallel ranges: the Greater Himalaya (Himadri) with peaks over 6,000 m, the Lesser Himalaya (Himachal) with hill stations such as Shimla and Mussoorie, and the Shiwaliks foothills, whose flat valleys are called duns (Dehradun). Beyond lie the cold deserts of Ladakh and the Karakoram . The Himalaya’s glaciers feed the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. Crops: apples, cherries and walnuts (Kashmir, Himachal), tea (Darjeeling), rice terraces, barley and buckwheat at altitude; saffron at Pampore in Kashmir. The Northeast hills (Patkai, Naga, Mizo, Garo–Khasi–Jaintia) are among the wettest and most biodiverse parts of India, with jhum (shifting) cultivation, tea in Assam’s Brahmaputra valley and the living root bridges of Meghalaya. 2. The Indo-Gangetic–Brahmaputra Plain # One of the largest and most fertile alluvial plains on Earth, formed by Himalayan rivers dumping sediment into a trough in front of the mountains. Subregions: the bhabar (pebbly foot of the hills, where streams vanish underground), the terai (marshy, now largely cleared), bhangar (older alluvium with lime nodules, kankar ) and khadar (new flood-renewed alluvium). This is India’s grain bowl: wheat and rice in Punjab and Haryana, sugarcane in western UP, rice and jute in Bihar, West Bengal and Assam. 3. The Thar Desert # Western Rajasthan’s sand dunes and rocky plains, with 100–500 mm of rain. See Deserts of the world . Crops: bajra, guar, moth bean, mustard and wheat where canals reach. 4. The Peninsular Plateau # India’s oldest land, a block of ancient crystalline rock (part of Gondwana) bordered by the Aravalli , Vindhya and Satpura ranges and the Western and Eastern Ghats . It contains: - the Central Highlands : Malwa plateau (black soil, soybeans, wheat), Bundelkhand (drought-prone), Chota Nagpur (minerals, red soils, tribal forests); - the Deccan Plateau : black cotton soil (regur) in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh grows cotton, soybeans, sorghum and pulses; red and laterite soils in Karnataka, Telangana and Tamil Nadu grow millets, groundnut and pulses. 5. The coastal plains # West coast: narrow and wet: the Konkan, Goa and the Malabar coast of Kerala, with lagoons and backwaters; rice, coconut, cashew, pepper, cardamom and rubber. East coast: broad, with the great deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri , the rice bowls of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Exposed to Bay of Bengal cyclones. 6. The islands # Andaman and Nicobar Islands: a chain of submerged mountains in the Bay of Bengal, mostly rainforest, with India’s only active volcano on Barren Island . Lakshadweep: coral atolls in the Arabian Sea, growing coconuts. Agro-climatic zones # India’s Planning Commission divided the country into 15 agro-climatic regions (Western Himalaya, Eastern Himalaya, Lower/Middle/Upper/Trans-Gangetic Plains, Eastern Plateau and Hills, Central, Western and Southern Plateau and Hills, East and West Coast Plains, Gujarat Plains and Hills, Western Dry Region, and the Islands) to plan crops by soil and rainfall. Related: Soils of India · Rainfall and the monsoon · India’s country profile Sources: NCERT: Contemporary India I, Ch. 2 Physical Features · Wikipedia: Geography of India

t: Climate Zones Explained: The Köppen System
d: How sunlight, latitude, mountains, oceans and wind divide the land into climate zones, and how the Köppen system names them.
x: Weather is what happens today; climate is the average over at least 30 years. Climates differ because of five controls: latitude (how directly the Sun shines), altitude , distance from the sea , ocean currents , and prevailing winds and pressure belts , plus mountains that block or lift those winds. The Köppen classification # Proposed by the German-Russian climatologist Wladimir Köppen in 1884 and refined with Rudolf Geiger, it groups climates by temperature and rainfall, because vegetation responds to both. Each climate has a letter code: Group Meaning Examples A Tropical Every month averages above 18 °C Af rainforest (Kerala hills, Amazon), Am monsoon (Mumbai coast), Aw savanna (most of peninsular India) B Dry Evaporation exceeds rainfall BWh hot desert (Thar), BWk cold desert (Ladakh), BSh semi-arid (interior Deccan) C Temperate Coldest month 0–18 °C Csa Mediterranean, Cfa humid subtropical, Cwa monsoon-influenced subtropical (Delhi, Lucknow), Cfb oceanic (London) D Continental Coldest month below 0 °C, warmest above 10 °C Dfa/Dfb (Ukraine, US Midwest), Dfc subarctic (Siberia) E Polar Warmest month below 10 °C ET tundra, EF ice cap H Highland Varies with altitude Himalaya, Andes Second and third letters show rainfall timing (f = wet all year, s = dry summer, w = dry winter, m = monsoon) and summer heat (a = hot, b = warm, c = cool, d = very cold winter). Average annual rainfall by climate type (mm) Tropical rainforest Tropical rainforest 2,500 mm Tropical monsoon Tropical monsoon 2,000 mm Humid subtropical Humid subtropical 1,300 mm Tropical savanna Tropical savanna 1,100 mm Oceanic Oceanic 900 mm Mediterranean Mediterranean 600 mm Semi-arid Semi-arid 450 mm Hot desert Hot desert 100 mm Source: Typical mid-range values of Köppen classes Global circulation in one picture # Sunlight heats the equator most. Hot air rises there (the rainy Intertropical Convergence Zone, ITCZ ), spreads poleward, sinks around 30° (dry deserts), and returns as the trade winds . Further out, westerlies bring storms to the mid-latitudes, and cold air sinks at the poles. The ITCZ shifts north and south with the seasons, and this movement, amplified by land heating, drives the monsoons . Climate zones are moving # A 1-km Köppen map by Beck and colleagues (2018) projected that by 2071–2100, under high emissions, a large share of land would shift to a different main climate class: tropical and dry zones expand, while polar and cold zones shrink. Farmers already see it: wine grapes now grow in southern England, apple growing in Himachal is moving uphill, and Mediterranean summers are drier. Browse all climate zones . Sources: Beck et al. 2018, Scientific Data · Wikipedia: Köppen climate classification

d: Why rain falls where it does, the world's wettest and driest places, how the Indian monsoon works, and how the 2026 monsoon ended 13% below normal.
x: Rain forms when moist air rises, cools and condenses. Air is lifted in three ways, and each makes a distinct rainfall pattern: Convectional rain: the Sun heats the ground, warm air shoots upward and builds afternoon thunderstorms. Typical of the equator and of Indian pre-monsoon storms ( kalbaisakhi in Bengal, mango showers in Kerala). Orographic (relief) rain: wind is forced up a mountain. The windward side is soaked and the leeward side lies in a rain shadow, as along the Western Ghats. Frontal (cyclonic) rain: warm air rides over cold air along a front, giving the steady rain of Europe and North America, and India’s winter western disturbances , which bring snow to the Himalaya and rain for the wheat crop. Wettest and driest places (average mm/yr) Mawsynram, India Mawsynram, India 11,871 mm Cherrapunji, India Cherrapunji, India 11,777 mm Lloró, Colombia Lloró, Colombia 12,717 mm Mumbai Mumbai 2,200 mm Delhi Delhi 780 mm London London 600 mm Cairo Cairo 25 mm Arica, Chile Arica, Chile 1 mm Source: Long-term station averages (WMO, IMD; rounded) The Indian monsoon # Monsoon comes from the Arabic mausim , “season”. In summer, the land of South Asia heats far faster than the Indian Ocean. Low pressure deepens over the northwest of the subcontinent, the ITCZ moves north to about 20–25°N, and moist southwesterly winds blow in from the ocean. The Tibetan Plateau, heated in summer, strengthens the circulation, and the Himalaya trap the moisture. How the season unfolds - **Onset:** the monsoon reaches Kerala around **1 June** and covers all India by about **8 July**. - **Two branches:** the *Arabian Sea branch* hits the Western Ghats; the *Bay of Bengal branch* swings up into the Northeast (Mawsynram, Cherrapunji) and then west along the Himalaya. - **Breaks:** dry spells of a week or more when the monsoon trough moves to the Himalayan foothills. - **Withdrawal:** from Rajasthan starting around 17 September, from the whole country by mid-October. - **Northeast (winter) monsoon:** October–December, bringing most of the year's rain to coastal Tamil Nadu. About 70–80% of India’s annual rainfall falls in June–September. More than half of India’s cropland is rain-fed, so a good monsoon boosts the kharif harvest (rice, cotton, soybeans, pulses) and refills reservoirs and groundwater for the rabi (winter) crop. What makes a monsoon good or bad # El Niño (warm eastern Pacific) tends to weaken the Indian monsoon; most major Indian droughts (1877, 1918, 1972, 1987, 2002, 2009) were El Niño years. La Niña tends to strengthen it. Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD): a warmer western Indian Ocean (positive IOD) can boost rainfall even in El Niño years, as in 1997. Snow cover over Eurasia and the Madden–Julian Oscillation also play a part. The 2026 monsoon # The India Meteorological Department reported that June–September 2026 rainfall was 87% of the long-period average : 759.4 mm against a normal of 868.6 mm, a “deficient” season. The shortfall was steepest in East and Northeast India (74%) and the South Peninsula (76%) . India's 2026 monsoon: rainfall as % of normal All India All India 87% South Peninsula South Peninsula 76% East & Northeast East & Northeast 74% Source: India Meteorological Department, end-of-season statement (Sept 2026) Changing rainfall # Total monsoon rainfall over India has not changed much in the long run, but its character has: fewer moderate rain days, more dry spells and more extreme downpours (over 150 mm a day), which cause floods such as Kerala 2018 and Wayanad 2024 and are hard for soils to absorb. Related: Droughts · Climate zones Sources: IMD: Monsoon season reports · Wikipedia: Monsoon of South Asia

d: Meteorological, agricultural, hydrological and socio-economic drought; what causes them; the worst droughts and famines in history; and how droughts are getting longer.
x: A drought is a long period of unusually low water supply. Unlike a flood or cyclone it creeps in slowly, has no clear start or end, and can cover whole continents. Droughts have become more frequent and longer by about 29% since 2000 , according to the UN, and together with land degradation they cost the world an estimated $878 billion a year . Four kinds of drought # From missing rain to empty plates 1. **Meteorological drought:** rainfall well below normal for a region. India's IMD calls a season "deficient" when all-India rain is below 90% of normal. 2. **Agricultural drought:** soil moisture too low for crops at a critical stage, such as flowering. It can happen even with near-normal rain if the rain arrives at the wrong time. 3. **Hydrological drought:** rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater fall low. It lags behind the rain deficit by months or years. 4. **Socio-economic drought:** demand for water outstrips supply, causing crop failure, livestock deaths, migration and sometimes famine. What causes drought # Ocean–atmosphere cycles: El Niño weakens the Indian and Southeast Asian monsoons and dries southern Africa and Australia; La Niña dries the Horn of Africa and the southwestern USA. Blocking high-pressure systems that park over a region for weeks. Land feedbacks: dry soil heats up and reduces local rain, deepening the drought. Human factors: groundwater overuse, deforestation, thirsty crops in dry places, and warming, which increases evaporation (so-called “hot droughts”). Droughts that changed history # Drought When What happened 4.2-kiloyear event ~2200 BCE A centuries-long dry spell linked to the decline of Egypt’s Old Kingdom, the Akkadian Empire and possibly the mature Harappan cities Great Famine (India) 1876–78 A strong El Niño failed the monsoon; 5.5–10 million died under colonial grain-export policies Dust Bowl (USA) 1930s Ploughed-up prairie blew away, displacing millions and creating the US Soil Conservation Service Sahel droughts 1968–1985 Decades of low rain across West Africa; ~100,000+ deaths and mass migration Maharashtra 1972 Led to India’s Employment Guarantee Scheme, the forerunner of MGNREGA Millennium Drought (Australia) 1997–2009 Rewrote water law in the Murray–Darling basin Syria 2006–2010 The worst drought in the instrumental record, made 2–3× more likely by warming (Kelley et al. 2015) Horn of Africa 2020–23 Five failed rainy seasons in a row, the longest on record there Southern Africa 2024 El Niño drought destroyed maize harvests across Zambia, Zimbabwe and Malawi Amazon 2023–24 Rio Negro at Manaus fell to its lowest level since 1902 Browse every drought and land disaster . How droughts are measured # SPI (Standardised Precipitation Index) compares rain with the long-term record. SPEI adds evaporation, so it captures heat-driven droughts. Soil moisture from satellites such as SMAP and SMOS. Vegetation health (NDVI) from MODIS and Sentinel. GRACE satellites weigh groundwater changes from orbit; they revealed the rapid depletion of northwest India’s aquifers. Coping with drought # Traditional systems such as stepwells, johads , kuls and tank cascades; watershed development (Ralegan Siddhi, Hiware Bazar); drought-tolerant crops (millets, sorghum, pulses); drip irrigation; crop insurance; early-warning systems; and employment guarantees that keep money flowing in bad years. Sources: UNCCD: Drought · Kelley et al. 2015, PNAS · Wikipedia: Drought

d: Land is warming faster than the global average. What that means for heat, rain, ice, forests, soils and crops, and how land can help fix the problem.
x: Since pre-industrial times, the land surface has warmed about 1.6 °C , considerably more than the global average (about 1.1–1.3 °C when oceans are included), because land has less water to evaporate and smaller heat capacity (IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land, 2019). What is changing # Seven big shifts 1. **Heat:** extreme heat is more frequent and intense. Heatwaves over 45 °C in northern India and Pakistan, and over 50 °C in the Middle East, now occur more often. 2. **Rain:** the water cycle intensifies. Wet extremes get wetter and dry spells longer; dry subtropics expand. 3. **Ice:** mountain glaciers lost 408 Gt in 2025 alone, and every glacier region has shrunk four years in a row. 4. **Permafrost** is thawing, releasing carbon. 5. **Fire:** fire seasons are longer, from Canada's record 2023 season to Australia's Black Summer. 6. **Seasons:** springs start earlier; crops and wild plants flower sooner; pests and diseases move to higher latitudes and altitudes. 7. **Soils:** warmer soils lose carbon faster, and heavier rain erodes them. Crops and food # Every 1 °C of global warming is estimated to cut global yields of maize by ~7.4% , wheat by ~6.0% , rice by ~3.2% and soybean by ~3.1% without adaptation (Zhao et al. 2017, PNAS). Wheat in north India is especially sensitive to heat in February–March at grain filling, as the March 2022 heatwave showed. Land is also part of the solution # Land absorbs roughly a third of the CO₂ humans emit each year, mostly in forests and soils, while agriculture, forestry and land use cause about 22% of greenhouse emissions (IPCC). Options include: - Stopping deforestation , as in the Amazon’s sharp decline in 2025–26; - Restoring degraded land and forests (the Bonn Challenge, Great Green Wall); - Building soil carbon through cover crops, reduced tillage, agroforestry and biochar; - Protecting peatlands and wetlands ; - Cutting food waste and shifting diets , which frees land. Related: Snow, ice and permafrost · Droughts · Land degradation Sources: IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land (2019) · Zhao et al. 2017, PNAS · WGMS

t: What Is Soil? How It Forms and Why It Matters
d: Soil is a living mix of minerals, water, air and organisms that takes centuries to form. Its layers, texture, the five factors that create it, and the 12 world soil orders.
x: Soil is the thin, loose layer at Earth’s surface where rock, air, water and life meet. A typical healthy soil is about 45% minerals, 25% water, 25% air and 5% organic matter by volume. One teaspoon can hold more microorganisms than there are people on Earth. Soil grows about 95% of our food , stores more carbon than the atmosphere and all plants combined, and filters most of our drinking water. How soil forms: five factors # Soil scientist Vasily Dokuchaev (Russia, 1880s) and later Hans Jenny (1941) described soil as the product of five factors, remembered as CLORPT : 1. Climate: rain and temperature control weathering and leaching. Hot, wet climates make deep red, leached soils; dry climates make thin, salty soils. 2. Organisms: plants, roots, fungi, bacteria, earthworms and termites mix and enrich soil. 3. Relief (topography): slopes lose soil downhill; valleys collect it. 4. Parent material: the rock or sediment underneath (basalt gives black soils; granite gives sandy red soils; river silt gives alluvium). 5. Time: forming just 2.5 cm (1 inch) of topsoil can take several hundred years . Soil layers (horizons) # Horizon Name What it is O Organic Leaf litter and humus A Topsoil Dark, mixed with organic matter, full of roots and life E Eluviated Leached, pale layer (common in forest soils) B Subsoil Collects clay, iron and minerals washed down from above C Parent material Weathered rock R Bedrock Solid rock Texture: sand, silt and clay # Particles are sorted by size: sand (2–0.05 mm, gritty, drains fast), silt (0.05–0.002 mm, smooth) and clay (under 0.002 mm, sticky, holds water and nutrients). A balanced mix is loam , the farmer’s ideal. Soil pH matters too: most crops prefer 6–7.5; tea and blueberries like acid soils; alkaline usar soils need gypsum. The world’s soil orders # The USDA Soil Taxonomy recognises 12 soil orders . The richest for farming are mollisols (grassland “black earths”) and andisols (volcanic ash). The most weathered and nutrient-poor are oxisols in the tropics. Browse them all in the soil catalog . Soil in numbers About a third of the world’s soils are moderately to highly degraded (FAO) Global soil erosion by water: ~36 billion tonnes a year (Borrelli et al. 2017) Soils hold about 1,500–2,400 billion tonnes of organic carbon in the top metre or two World Soil Day: 5 December Next: Soils of India . Sources: FAO: Status of the World’s Soil Resources · USDA NRCS: Soil Taxonomy · Borrelli et al. 2017

d: India's eight major soil groups (alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid, saline, peaty and forest soils): where they occur, how they formed and what they grow.
x: The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) classifies India’s soils into eight major groups. Together they explain why Punjab grows wheat, Maharashtra grows cotton, Kerala grows rubber and Rajasthan grows bajra. Soil Share of India (approx.) Main areas Main crops Alluvial ~40% Indo-Gangetic plain, deltas, coastal strips Rice, wheat, sugarcane, jute, pulses Red and yellow ~18% Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand Millets, groundnut, pulses, cotton Black (regur) ~15% Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Telangana Cotton, soybeans, sorghum, wheat, sugarcane Arid (desert) ~4% Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana Bajra, guar, pulses Laterite ~3.7% Western Ghats, Kerala, Odisha, Northeast Cashew, tea, coffee, rubber Saline and alkaline ~1.3% Punjab, Haryana, UP, Gujarat coast, Sundarbans Salt-tolerant rice and barley after reclamation Peaty and marshy small Kerala (Kuttanad), Sundarbans, Odisha coast Rice Forest and mountain ~8% Himalaya, Western Ghats Tea, fruit, spices Alluvial soils # Laid down by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems and coastal rivers. Khadar (new alluvium) is renewed by floods every year and is very fertile; bhangar (old alluvium) lies above flood level and contains lime nodules ( kankar ). Rich in potash, often low in nitrogen and phosphorus. These soils feed most of India. Black cotton soil (regur) # Formed from the weathering of the Deccan Traps basalt. Rich in clay, calcium, magnesium and potash; poor in nitrogen and phosphorus. It swells when wet and cracks deeply when dry, so it “ploughs itself” by mixing as cracks fill. It holds moisture for months, which suits rain-fed cotton. Hard to work when wet (“sticky”) or very dry. Red and yellow soils # Developed on old crystalline rocks (granite, gneiss) in low-rainfall parts of the plateau. The red colour comes from iron oxide; yellow where the iron is hydrated. Porous and light, low in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus; productive with fertiliser and irrigation. Laterite soils # From the Latin later , “brick”. Formed under heavy rain and high temperature, which leach away silica and leave iron and aluminium. Acidic and poor, but excellent for tree crops such as cashew, tea, coffee and rubber. Freshly cut laterite hardens in air and has been used as building stone for centuries (temples in Kerala and Odisha, houses in Goa and Konkan). Arid soils # Sandy, light-coloured, saline in places, with a calcium carbonate ( kankar ) layer that blocks water. Low in organic matter. Turn productive with irrigation, as along the Indira Gandhi Canal. Saline and alkaline soils # Known locally as reh , kallar or usar . Salt rises with groundwater in poorly drained, over-irrigated land, or is left by seawater on coasts. Reclaimed with gypsum , drainage, salt-tolerant varieties (such as CSR rice from the Central Soil Salinity Research Institute, Karnal) and green manure. Soil health in India # The national Soil Health Card scheme, launched in 2015, has tested farmers’ fields for 12 parameters and recommended fertiliser doses. Common problems are low organic carbon (often below 0.5%), nitrogen deficiency, zinc deficiency and fertiliser imbalance (too much urea relative to phosphorus and potash). d: Up to 40% of the world's land is degraded. The causes (erosion, salinity, nutrient loss, overgrazing, deforestation), the 2026 UNCCD COP17 in Mongolia, and the restoration successes that show it can be reversed.
x: Land degradation is the long-term loss of the land’s ability to produce food, store water and support life. When it happens in drylands it is called desertification . It does not mean deserts marching forward like sand waves; it is patchy decline driven mostly by how people use land, made worse by drought. The scale of the problem Up to 40% of the world’s land is degraded, and droughts have grown in frequency and duration by 29% since 2000 (UN, at UNCCD COP17, Mongolia, August 2026) Land degradation and drought cost about $878 billion a year ; Sub-Saharan Africa holds 45% of the world’s degraded land About 3.2 billion people are affected (IPBES 2018) India: about 97.85 million hectares (~30% of its area) was undergoing degradation in 2018–19 (ISRO’s Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas, 2021) Where the world's degraded land is Sub-Saharan Africa: 45 Rest of the world: 55 100 ■ Sub-Saharan Africa — 45 (45%) ■ Rest of the world — 55 (55%) UNCCD / Down To Earth, 2026: land degradation and drought cost ~$878 bn a year. Causes # What degrades land - **Water erosion:** rain washes topsoil off bare or ploughed slopes. The main process in India. - **Wind erosion:** dry, bare soil blows away (the Dust Bowl, the Thar margins). - **Salinisation and waterlogging:** irrigation without drainage raises salty groundwater (Punjab, Haryana, Indus basin, Aral Sea basin). - **Nutrient mining and loss of organic matter:** taking crops off year after year without returning residues or manure. - **Overgrazing:** too many animals strip grasslands bare. - **Deforestation:** removes roots that hold soil and the litter that feeds it. - **Compaction** by heavy machines; **sealing** by roads and buildings; **mining**. - **Pollution:** heavy metals, plastics and excess agrochemicals. UNCCD and COP17 # The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) , adopted in 1994, is one of the three “Rio conventions” (with climate and biodiversity). Its 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) concluded in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, in August 2026 , focusing on rangelands, drought resilience and finance for land restoration. Countries have pledged to restore about 1 billion hectares by 2030; India pledged 26 million hectares . Restoration that works # Loess Plateau, China: terracing, banning grazing on slopes and replanting turned one of the world’s most eroded landscapes green, raising incomes for about 2.5 million people. Farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR), Niger: farmers protected tree stumps sprouting in their fields, regreening around 5 million hectares. Zaï pits and stone bunds (Burkina Faso): small planting pits filled with manure catch rainwater and revive crusted soils. Great Green Wall: a mosaic of restoration across the Sahel, from Senegal to Djibouti. India: watershed villages such as Ralegan Siddhi and Hiware Bazar (Maharashtra) recharged groundwater with check dams and grazing rules; reclamation of usar land in UP with gypsum; Rajasthan’s johad revival led by Tarun Bharat Sangh revived the Arvari river. Browse droughts and land disasters . Sources: UNCCD · ISRO SAC: Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas of India · IPBES Land Degradation Assessment 2018

d: About 12,000 years ago people in at least eleven places independently began to farm. Where, why, which plants and animals were tamed first, and how farming changed humanity.
x: For around 300,000 years Homo sapiens lived by hunting, fishing and gathering. Then, after the last Ice Age ended about 11,700 years ago , the climate became warmer, wetter and more stable, and in several regions people began to plant and herd. This Neolithic Revolution was not a single event but a slow shift over thousands of years. The centres of domestication # Region When (approx.) First crops and animals Fertile Crescent (Iraq, Syria, Turkey, Iran, Levant) 11,500–10,000 years ago Emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils, peas, chickpeas, flax; sheep, goats, cattle, pigs China : Yangtze and Yellow River ~9,000 years ago Rice (Yangtze); foxtail and broomcorn millet (Yellow River); pigs, chickens New Guinea highlands (Kuk Swamp) ~7,000–10,000 years ago Taro, bananas, sugarcane Mesoamerica (southern Mexico) ~9,000 years ago Maize (from teosinte), squash, beans, chillies Andes and Amazonia ~8,000–10,000 years ago Potatoes, quinoa, cassava, peanuts; llamas, alpacas, guinea pigs Eastern North America ~5,000 years ago Sunflower, squash, goosefoot Sahel and West Africa ~5,000–3,000 years ago Sorghum, pearl millet, African rice, yams, cowpeas Ethiopian Highlands ~4,000+ years ago Teff, coffee, finger millet, enset Indian subcontinent ~9,000 years ago (Mehrgarh) Barley, wheat (from the west), zebu cattle; later rice, mung bean, urad, sesame, cotton, pigeon pea India’s first farmers # Mehrgarh in Balochistan (now Pakistan), settled about 7000 BCE , is one of the earliest farming villages in South Asia, growing barley and wheat and herding humped zebu cattle , which were domesticated locally. Later, sites in the Ganga valley such as Lahuradewa show early rice use, and the Harappan (Indus) civilisation, from about 2600 BCE, grew wheat, barley, peas, sesame and, famously, some of the earliest cotton for textiles. Pigeon pea, mung and urad beans and millets were domesticated in peninsular India. How a wild plant becomes a crop # Early farmers unknowingly selected for the domestication syndrome : - seeds that stay on the plant instead of shattering (so they can be harvested); - larger seeds and fruits; - plants that ripen together; - less bitterness and fewer toxins; - loss of seed dormancy, so seeds sprout when sown. Maize is the extreme case: its wild ancestor teosinte has a few hard kernels on a tiny spike. Consequences # Farming produced surplus food, permanent villages, rising populations, the first cities, writing, taxes, armies, and specialised crafts. It also brought harder work, poorer early diets, crowd diseases caught from animals (measles, smallpox, influenza) and inequality. Over the following millennia farming transformed about half of the planet’s habitable land. Related: Crops and climate · Crop catalog Sources: Diamond 2002, Nature · Wikipedia: Neolithic Revolution · Wikipedia: Mehrgarh

t: Which Crops Grow Where, and Why
d: Each crop has a climate, soil and water "comfort zone". How temperature, rainfall, day length and soil decide the world's crop map, with India's kharif, rabi and zaid seasons.
x: A crop grows best where its needs match the land: enough warmth for its season, water at the right time, suitable soil and the right day length . Change any of these and yields drop. Green Revolution breeders deliberately made varieties day-neutral so they could grow across latitudes. With warming, crop belts are shifting: maize and soybeans are spreading north in Canada and Russia, apple orchards in Himachal are moving uphill, and coffee may lose up to half of its suitable land by 2050 in some projections. t: Fruits of the World and Where They Grow
d: Tropical, subtropical, Mediterranean and temperate fruits, their wild origins, the climate each needs, and India's place as the world's second-largest fruit producer.
x: Fruits are the seed-bearing parts of flowering plants, and the ones we eat have mostly been bred over thousands of years from wild ancestors scattered across the world. Where a fruit grows depends above all on winter cold : tropical fruits die with frost, while temperate fruits need a winter chilling period to flower properly. Four fruit belts # From the equator to the cool temperate zone - **Tropical** (no frost, warm all year): mango, banana, papaya, pineapple, jackfruit, coconut, durian, mangosteen, guava. Grown across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, Central and South America and Africa. - **Subtropical** (mild winters, occasional light frost): citrus (orange, lemon, lime), lychee, pomegranate, avocado, guava. Nagpur (oranges), Bihar (lychee), Maharashtra (pomegranate), Brazil, Spain, Florida. - **Mediterranean** (hot dry summers, wet mild winters): grapes, olives, figs, almonds, dates (in the hot desert margins), apricots. - **Temperate** (cold winters, needing roughly 800–1,500 chilling hours below 7 °C for many apple varieties): apples, pears, cherries, plums, peaches, walnuts, strawberries, blueberries. Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, China, Europe and North America. Where favourite fruits came from # Mango: northeastern India and Myanmar; cultivated in India for over 4,000 years. Banana: New Guinea and Southeast Asia; the seedless edible banana is a hybrid of Musa acuminata and M. balbisiana . Apple: the wild apple forests of the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan; spread along the Silk Road. Citrus: the foothills of the eastern Himalaya, Assam, Myanmar and southern China. Grapes: the Caucasus, where wine-making goes back 8,000 years (Georgia). Avocado and cacao: Mesoamerica and the upper Amazon. India and fruit # India is the world’s second-largest fruit producer after China and the largest producer of mangoes, bananas, papayas and guavas . Notable regional fruits: Alphonso (Ratnagiri), Kesar (Gujarat) and Dasheri (Malihabad) mangoes; Nagpur oranges; Muzaffarpur shahi lychee; Kashmiri and Himachal apples; Nashik grapes; Solapur pomegranates; Jalgaon bananas; and the jamun , amla , ber , bael and karonda of Indian forests and drylands, often hardier and more nutritious than exotics. Browse the fruit catalog . Sources: National Horticulture Board, India · FAO: FAOSTAT · Wikipedia: Mango

t: The Green Revolution and Food Security
d: How high-yielding seeds, irrigation and fertiliser took India from famine to surplus, the problems they created for soil and water, and how the world can feed 10 billion people.
x: In the mid-1960s India was importing millions of tonnes of wheat under the US PL-480 programme after back-to-back droughts in 1965 and 1966 . Within a decade it was self-sufficient in grain. The change is called the Green Revolution . What changed # The package - **High-yielding varieties (HYVs):** semi-dwarf wheat bred by **Norman Borlaug** at CIMMYT in Mexico, and semi-dwarf rice such as **IR8** from IRRI in the Philippines. Short, stiff stems carried heavy grain heads without falling over. - **Irrigation:** canals and, above all, millions of tube wells. - **Chemical fertilisers and pesticides.** - **Policy:** guaranteed minimum support prices (MSP), government procurement (FCI, 1965), credit and agricultural universities (Pantnagar, Ludhiana). In India the effort was led by **M. S. Swaminathan**, agriculture minister **C. Subramaniam** and Prime Ministers Lal Bahadur Shastri and Indira Gandhi. India’s wheat production rose from about 12 million tonnes (1964–65) to over 110 million tonnes in recent years, and rice from about 39 to over 130 million tonnes. Punjab, Haryana and western UP became the national granary. The costs # Groundwater: satellites showed northwest India losing about 17.7 km³ of groundwater a year (Rodell et al. 2009), driven by free electricity and water-hungry paddy in a semi-arid region. Water tables in parts of Punjab fall about 0.5–1 m a year. Soil: declining organic carbon, micronutrient (zinc) deficiencies, salinity and waterlogging. Diversity: traditional varieties and millets were displaced; diets shifted toward rice and wheat. Air: stubble burning after the rice harvest adds to north India’s winter smog. Inequality: irrigated regions and larger farmers gained most at first. Pingali (2012) concluded that the Green Revolution averted famine and spared vast areas of forest from being cleared, but that the next stage must focus on water, soils and nutrition. Feeding 10 billion # The world already produces enough calories for everyone, yet about 700 million people go hungry because of poverty, conflict and waste. Researchers (Foley et al. 2011) point to five strategies: stop expanding farmland into forests; close yield gaps; use water and fertiliser more efficiently; shift diets; and cut food waste (about a third of food is lost or wasted). In India, current efforts include crop diversification away from paddy in Punjab, the revival of millets (2023 was the UN International Year of Millets, proposed by India), natural and zero-budget farming trials, micro-irrigation and the Soil Health Card . Sources: Pingali 2012, PNAS · Rodell et al. 2009, Nature · Foley et al. 2011, Nature · Wikipedia: Green Revolution in India

Status date: 15 November 2026 . # Stream Status Next milestone 1 Amazon deforestation (Brazil) 3,335 km² cleared Aug 2025–Jul 2026, −41.8%, lowest since 1988 Final PRODES figure; Cerrado down ~24% 2 India monsoon 2026 87% of long-period average (deficient) Rabi sowing and reservoir levels; 2027 forecast in April 3 Global glacier loss 408 ± 132 Gt lost in 2025; all 19 regions shrank for the 4th year WGMS 2026 data 4 Desertification (UNCCD COP17) COP17 concluded in Mongolia, Aug 2026; up to 40% of land degraded 2030 restoration targets 5 Drought cost ~$878 billion a year Drought-resilience finance 6 Soil health About a third of soils degraded (FAO) World Soil Day, 5 Dec 1 · Amazon deforestation (Brazil) **Status:** Brazil's PRODES satellite system measured **3,335 km²** of clear-cutting in the Amazon between August 2025 and July 2026, a **41.8% fall** and the lowest since records began in 1988. The faster DETER alert system recorded about 2,874 km² (down ~36%). Clearing in the **Cerrado** savanna fell about 24% to ~5,517 km². **Why it matters:** the Amazon stores roughly 150–200 billion tonnes of carbon and recycles much of South America's rainfall. Parts of the southeastern Amazon already emit more carbon than they absorb. **Next:** the consolidated PRODES figure and whether the trend holds through the dry season and the 2026 Brazilian political cycle. Sources: [INPE TerraBrasilis](https://terrabrasilis.dpi.inpe.br/) · [Amazon rainforest catalog entry](/wiki/landforms/amazon-rainforest.html) 2 · India monsoon 2026 **Status:** June–September rainfall was **759.4 mm vs a normal of 868.6 mm (87%)**. East & Northeast India received 74% and the South Peninsula 76% of normal. **Next:** effects on the rabi (winter) crop, reservoir storage and groundwater; IMD's first 2027 forecast in April. Sources: [IMD](https://mausam.imd.gov.in/) · [Rainfall and the monsoon](/wiki/climate/rainfall-and-the-monsoon.html) 3 · Global glacier loss **Status:** Glaciers lost **408 ± 132 Gt** in hydrological year 2025 (~1.1 mm of sea-level rise). Loss rose from under 100 Gt a year (1976–1995) to ~390 Gt a year (2016–2025); cumulative loss since 1975 is ~9,583 Gt (26.4 mm). 2025 was the 4th consecutive year with mass loss in all 19 glacier regions. Sources: [WGMS](https://wgms.ch/global-glacier-state/) · [Copernicus Climate Change Service](https://climate.copernicus.eu/) · [Snow, ice and permafrost](/wiki/earth/snow-ice-and-permafrost.html) 4 · Desertification (UNCCD COP17) **Status:** COP17 of the UN Convention to Combat Desertification concluded in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, in August 2026. The UN says up to **40%** of land is degraded and droughts have become **29% more frequent and longer since 2000**. Sources: [UNCCD](https://www.unccd.int/) · [Land degradation](/wiki/soil/land-degradation-and-desertification.html) 5 · Drought cost **Status:** Land degradation and drought cost about **$878 billion a year**; Sub-Saharan Africa holds 45% of the world's degraded land. Sources: [UNCCD](https://www.unccd.int/land-and-life/drought/overview) · [Droughts](/wiki/climate/droughts.html) 6 · Soil health **Status:** FAO's *Status of the World's Soil Resources* found about a third of soils moderately to highly degraded. India's Soil Health Card scheme continues field testing. Sources: [FAO Global Soil Partnership](https://www.fao.org/global-soil-partnership/en/) · [What is soil?](/wiki/soil/what-is-soil.html)
